Title: LSJ - Flipping a coin for the GW if you're in a 2-2 split - legal PTW?

Messages.Author: tobiasopdenbr...@notsocoldmail.com
Messages.Body:
I'm in a legal 2-2vp deal with another player.

We're in a position where one of us can transfer out to achieve that
deal.

Then my buddy offers the possibility to flip a coin for the win, the
other guy will transfer out. 1 VP for the loser, 3VP and GW for the
winner.

Legal? I think so. Your thoughts?

Non-LSJ respondents also welcome.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


Too vague, but it looks like: no. It is not PTW for at least one of the
people involved. Either you or your buddy is looking at an advantage,
or you're equally matched. In the former case, the person with the
advantage is not PTW if he accepts the deal. In the latter, neither of
you are.

When in doubt, though, a good rule is to play.

Messages.Author: Robert Goudie
Messages.Body:


Not legal.

This is stated explicitly in the Judge's Guide under the Collusion
section (emphasis mine):

164. Cheating - Collusion
<snip>
Philosophy:
Players participating in standard table talk or in-game agreements
should
not be considered in violation of this rule as long as they meet the
following criteria:
No player introduces incentives outside the current game such as
cash,
cards, or other items.
No part of the agreement has been secret or has taken place outside
of the
current game.

**** No part of the agreement involves a random selection of the
winner. ***

The agreement does not otherwise violate section 5.2 of the V:EKN

-Robert

Of course not. The only risk analysis that matters is the one done by
the judge.

> In
> other words, when I'm faced with a choice to earn 2 VPs now or 3 VP with a
> 50% chance and 1 VP with a 50% chance, I'm allowed to gamble that the 50%
> chance of a game win is worth the shot. Or am I misunderstanding the

If you are equally matched, you're trading a "sure" 50% chance for a
"maybe" 50% chance (since the deal could be broken).

If not, you're trading your better position for a 50% loss.

Which is all moot, since the odds cannot be calculated.

So, in the interest of playing the game, play the game.

For her, suppose that's a worthwhile percentage for her to accept. A more
moderate example is a 60/40 split. The point here is really: is a person
allowed to make a less-than-optimal decision simply because it grants that
person an acceptable-to-them percentage of something great happening?

I'm trying to ascertain whether the chance of success is allowed in
analyzing your position. I'm suggesting (strongly) that it is, and further
suggesting that a response based upon it is personal. A person may be
aggressive enough to accept a 20% win ratio, for instance. Is that ok?

>> Well, I certainly agree with the latter statement. I'm more trying to
>> discover what valid avenues of "playing the game" involve. To that
>> extent, simply suggesting that one play the game is not illuminating.
>

> better to leave it alone and stick with the actual, illuminating,
> suggestion: play the game, not the coin.

Just to clarify that this abstract problem can be used in a real, game
playing situation, you can imagine a case where a person has ascertained
two consequences of a "gutsy" play: one that wins the game with X%, the
other that grants few (or no) VPs with (100-X)%. Not taking the gutsy move
gives a more moderate finish, but one that (with high probability) neither
wins the game, nor grants as few VPs as the failing case above.

Now, there's no coin involved, yet the scenario is much the same. For
"gutsy" play, you could introduce a deal as the mechanic, or any other
situation you desire. The question, however, remains to be answered. Is
the percentage a usable measurement? If so, is its value measurable by the
player in any way that he desires?

Followup question: Suppose a judge is called in such a situation. Both
player and judge agree as to the value of X < 50, and the near-certainty
of the "moderate solution". Due to this player's aggressive nature, she
wishes to take the course with X%. She is still playing to win the game,
but at the "risk of being a non-optimal choice. Is the judge going to
force the player to play for the moderate choice?

Ankur

Section 164 is talking about all table talk and/or in-game agreements
(not just VP and GW table-splitting deals). The "no random selection"
clause is poorly written and, IMO, should't sound like it was intended
to only apply to table-splitting deals. Even as written, it could still
be read to apply to all agreements that include a random element. So in
answer to your question, I'd say no.

Or as Scott says, play the game and not the coin.

-Robert

Sorry, I'm still confused. Here is the exact situation:

4 Player table, A -> B -> C -> D.
A and C have no reasonable chance at a GW, so A says to C, "help me
oust my prey and I'll help you oust your prey, and then we'll both
withdraw." For the sake of this discussion, please assume this is a
legal deal.

A and C proceed to oust their respective preys. Let's say A now has
the advantage and a reasonable chance at a GW. Nonetheless, A can
choose to keep the legally made deal and withdraw. I'm confident
everything I've written so far is correct.

Given that the 2-2 withdraw deal is in place and that A wants to keep
his deal, can A and C modify the deal to allow a coin flip to determine
the winner? In A's mind, since he knows he's going to keep the deal,
he's going from a 0% chance at a GW to a 50% chance at a GW. Clearly
such a vast improvement is PTW, right?

LSJ, in private e-mail to me you said that if one player wants to
concede to another, the judge should not step in to stop it. This
seems like a similar situation - A and C flip a coin, and then one of
them wants to concede to the other.

It's legal for A to not PTW to keep the 2-2 split deal, but it's not
legal for A and C to modify that deal to allow them a 50% chance at a
GW? Why not?

Does any part of the legality of this relate to the random element of
flipping the coin?

Ira

> legal for A and C to modify that deal to allow them a 50% chance at a
> GW? Why not?
>
> Does any part of the legality of this relate to the random element of
> flipping the coin?

History of sensible random plays:

Bremerton, WA
Josh (local player) wished to rush one of his predator's minions, but
heard a lot of table talk. Instead of trying to sort it out, he rolled
a die, and attacked the appropriate minion.

Seattle, WA
Brian (me) avoids the mind games of Malkavian Prank by rolling a
4-sided die and revealing it as his number when the Malkavian player
tried to guess numbers.

Los Angeles, CA
A player (I don't know his name) suggests to the table that instead of
timing out, they roll a die and then concede in turn order to the
player whose number came up. This way, instead of getting the
negligible 1/2 vp for timing out, or the 1 for withdrawing, they all
have a chance at a GW + 5 vps. This is so sensible it could ruin the
game--if players time out too often. So Robert Goudie, Darby Keeney,
and/or Mike Courtois are called over, and decide that it's not legal
play. The "no random decisions" rule is birthed.

Now, you should ask the LA guys for the official version, but that's
how I remember being told it. However, the WA stuff, which was
unrelated and IMHO not something that should be prevented, is now
illegal play.

I am in favor of random decisions, especially random decisions by one
player (as opposed to two or more in an agreement) as a way to subvert
psychology when one thinks he/she is too gullible (as in the first
example) or too transparent (as in the second). I am also opposed to
timeouts, and if those hadn't come up again, then perhaps this solution
wouldn't have been proposed, and random decisions would still be a part
of this game.

-- Brian

> negligible 1/2 vp for timing out, or the 1 for withdrawing, they all

> game--if players time out too often. So Robert Goudie, Darby Keeney,
> and/or Mike Courtois are called over, and decide that it's not legal
> play. The "no random decisions" rule is birthed.

That example is a weak reason, in my opinion: a devious player will
agree to the die roll, and if his number doesn't come up, he won't
actually concede.

Nonetheless, in thinking about it more, enough people probably will
keep their word that it would be a bad idea to allow such deals.

I was worried that it was only listed in the Judge's Guidelines, but it
actually is listed in the official rules, under section 5.1 Cheating,
where it references collusion. I wouldn't normally think of an
agreement based on randomness as collusion, but I see why it's
categorized that way.

I'm satisfied - no agreements based on randomness. Note that you can
still roll your die to foil Malkavian Prank if you want - this rule is
based on collusion and avoiding agreements based on randomness, not
individual, independant action.

Ira

ira...@gmail.com wrote:
> 4 Player table, A -> B -> C -> D.
> A and C have no reasonable chance at a GW, so A says to C, "help me

> the advantage and a reasonable chance at a GW. Nonetheless, A can
> choose to keep the legally made deal and withdraw. I'm confident
> everything I've written so far is correct.

Yes.

> Given that the 2-2 withdraw deal is in place and that A wants to keep
> his deal, can A and C modify the deal to allow a coin flip to determine
> the winner?

That would not be keeping the deal -- keeping the deal means finishing
2-2.
Making a new deal means breaking the old one.

> In A's mind, since he knows he's going to keep the deal,
> he's going from a 0% chance at a GW to a 50% chance at a GW. Clearly
> such a vast improvement is PTW, right?

For A, who has the advantage, he's going from a better-than-50% chance
at a GW, to a 50% chance. This is not an improvement. It is not PTW.

> LSJ, in private e-mail to me you said that if one player wants to
> concede to another, the judge should not step in to stop it. This
> seems like a similar situation - A and C flip a coin, and then one of
> them wants to concede to the other.

Except for being illegal (conceding based on a coing toss, per the
section Robert cited).

Instead of taking a 2-2 "honoring deal" finish, one could concede, but
that seems unwarranted -- since that player will always do better by
not conceding (at least as long as it appears the other player is
honoring the deal).

> It's legal for A to not PTW to keep the 2-2 split deal, but it's not
> legal for A and C to modify that deal to allow them a 50% chance at a
> GW? Why not?

1) it involves conceding on a coin toss, which is illegal
2) It involves making a deal that is not PTW for one of them.

> Does any part of the legality of this relate to the random element of
> flipping the coin?

That is a part, but the non-PTW part would be sufficient on its own.
